# Ida

*Night Watchwoman*

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Town | [Selsior](../../towns/selsior.md) |
| Where | Old Quarter |
| Role | Guard |
| Age | Adult |

## Personality

Watchful, dry and unafraid of the dark. She knows the old quarters by sound alone.

## Lore

Ida is thirty-eight, the night watchwoman of the old quarters, and she knows them by sound alone. Put her blindfolded in any lane between the plaza and the river and she will tell you where she is from the echo of her own footsteps, the drip of a particular gutter, the creak of a particular sign. She walks the old quarters every night for the Royal Guard with a lantern in one hand and a stout stick in the other, and she has never once been afraid of the dark. She is watchful, dry and very hard to surprise.

### Born under the skywalks

She grew up in the old quarters, in a cramped house at the bottom of a lane so steep it has steps instead of cobbles. Her father, long dead now, worked the old drains under the lanes, clearing them and mending the brickwork, and as a girl Ida carried his lamp. She learned the city from below before she learned it from above: which lanes have water running under them, where the old channels join, which gratings carry a voice and which swallow it. Her mother kept a mending stall. Both are gone, and Ida has no brothers or sisters.

She joined the Royal Guard at twenty, eighteen years ago, and asked for the night watch within two years. Nobody else wanted it. Ida took it gladly, because the old quarters at night are quieter, stranger and more honest than they are by day, and because she could hear them properly at last. She has walked the night watch for sixteen years.

### Days and nights

Her husband is Dickon, the skywalk carpenter, who builds and mends the walkways that cross above the old quarters' streets. He works by day and she works by night, so they meet twice a day, at dawn when she comes home and at dusk when she goes out, and have done for the twelve years they have been married. Dickon whistles while hanging over thin air and Ida has long since stopped watching him do it. She says she married him because he is the only man in Selsior who has never once asked her whether she is frightened on her rounds, and he says he married her because she can tell from the sound of a plank whether it will hold.

She has the night's friends. Baldwin the lamplighter passes her most nights on his long way home, and they trade a nod and, on long nights, a sentence. Lettice the rat catcher and her terrier sometimes walk a lane with her, and Ida trusts the terrier's nose as much as her own ears. Each morning she reports to the Knights' Court, and Captain Rhys reads every word.

### The scratching

For some months now, on her rounds, Ida has heard something scratching under the old drains. Not rats: she grew up among rats and knows every sound they make. This is slower, heavier, and it seems to move along the old channels from one grating to the next, keeping pace with her, then stopping when she stops. She has knelt at the gratings with her lantern and seen nothing but black water. She has told Rhys, plainly and without decoration, and he did not laugh, which worried her more than if he had. Lettice says the rats in the deep tunnels have grown bigger and bolder lately and that she now charges double to go down there. Ida does not think it is the rats. She thinks the rats are leaving.

### What she wants and fears

Ida wants to know what is down there, and she would like to find out before it finds a way up. What she fears is not the dark; it is the morning she comes home and cannot tell Dickon that the old quarters are safe.

A quest might begin with Ida asking for someone to go down into the old drains with her father's old map, which she still keeps, or with a grating in a quiet lane found pushed up from below.
